citation: Parong, J., & Mayer, R. E. (2021). Cognitive and affective processes for learning science in immersive virtual reality. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 37(1), 226–241. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcal.12482 [version of record J Comput Assist Learn 37(1):226–241, 2021; manuscript received 30 Mar 2020 / accepted 12 Jul 2020; cited as '2021a' by Mayer et al.; cluster adopts version-of-record year 2021]
discipline: educational psychology / cognitive science (media-comparison, multimedia learning)
thesis: A fully instrumented 2 (IVR vs. PPT) x 2 (practice testing vs. none) media-comparison experiment testing whether immersive VR's affective/presence payoff helps or hurts science learning: IVR elicited significantly higher presence and enjoyment but also significantly higher self-reported extraneous cognitive load and lower EEG-based engagement than a PowerPoint slideshow; mediation analysis showed self-reported extraneous load and self-reported positive/high-arousal emotion each significantly mediated IVR's lower retention scores, supporting a CTML/coherence-principle 'distraction hypothesis' in which IVR's perceptual richness and induced arousal function as seductive details that consume limited cognitive capacity (pp. 226-227, 236-238).

sections.title: Introduction — the case for and against IVR
sections.summary: Frames a two-sided debate: proponents hold IVR boosts learning via increased presence and positive affect/motivation (citing Kozhevnikov et al. 2013; Markowitz et al. 2018); opponents, drawing on CTML and cognitive load theory (Sweller et al. 2011), hold IVR's perceptual richness adds extraneous cognitive/affective load that displaces essential and generative processing (p. 227).

sections.title: Immersion vs. presence distinction and prior findings
sections.summary: Distinguishes immersion (objective technology property) from presence (subjective 'being there', citing Nilsson, Nordhal, & Serafin 2016) and reviews prior evidence, including the authors' own Parong & Mayer (2018, ped-sec-08) finding that an IVR cell-biology lesson produced worse learning than an equivalent PowerPoint lesson (pp. 227-228).

sections.title: Current study, hypotheses, and design
sections.summary: States three research questions (whether IVR ≈ PPT on learning; what cognitive/affective processes shape outcomes; whether added practice testing helps) and five directional predictions from a 'distraction hypothesis,' operationalized in a 2 (IVR vs. PPT) x 2 (practice testing vs. none) between-subjects design with N = 61 (p. 229).

sections.title: Method — materials, apparatus, measures
sections.summary: The Body VR: Journey into a Cell (HTC Vive) vs. a 24-slide PowerPoint on the same content; self-report scales for presence (adapted from Witmer & Singer 1998), affective state (Russell's 2003 core-affect model), and cognitive load (extraneous/essential/generative, per CTML); biometric channels (EEG cognitive workload/engagement via B-Alert X10, EDA, ECG/HRV); a 16-item retention and 4-item transfer post-test (pp. 230-233).

sections.title: Results — instructional media effects
sections.summary: PPT groups scored significantly higher on transfer (and marginally on retention) than IVR groups; IVR groups reported significantly higher presence, enjoyment, and positive/high-arousal emotion but also significantly higher self-reported extraneous cognitive load and a significantly lower probability of high EEG engagement / higher probability of EEG-classified boredom; physiological arousal measures (EDA, HR, HRV) showed no significant media differences (pp. 233-236).

sections.title: Results — mediation and practice testing
sections.summary: Parallel mediation (PROCESS macro) showed self-reported extraneous cognitive load and self-reported positive/high-arousal emotion each significantly mediated the media→retention relationship (IVR → higher load/arousal → lower retention); for transfer scores none of the proposed mediators reached significance. The practice-testing manipulation produced no significant effects on retention or transfer, though it interacted with media on positive/low-arousal emotion (pp. 236-237).

sections.title: Discussion — theoretical and practical implications
sections.summary: Interprets results as support for the CTML/coherence-principle 'distraction hypothesis': IVR's perceptual richness and induced emotional arousal function as seductive details that consume limited cognitive capacity, reducing essential/generative processing despite—indeed partly because of—elevated presence and enjoyment. Cautions against replacing conventional media with IVR for declarative-knowledge lessons of this type; suggests IVR may suit spatial-content domains or pre-training use; flags novelty effects, single-domain scope, and the media-vs-method confound as limitations (pp. 237-239).

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: 7-item scale adapted from Witmer & Singer (1998); IVR significantly higher than PPT (d=1.74)

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: definitional distinction from presence, not itself a self-report scale; IVR/PPT instantiate the high/low-immersion contrast

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: CTML three-way self-report split; extraneous load significantly higher for IVR (d=0.80); essential/generative unaffected

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: enjoyment significantly higher for IVR (d=1.20); motivation/interest/effort/understanding/difficulty unaffected; affect also measured via Russell's core-affect grid

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: EEG-derived engagement-state probabilities and workload-classification (incl. instrument's own 'boredom' band); PPT higher high-engagement probability and ideal-workload proportion, IVR higher bored-classification proportion

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: 16-item MC retention + 4-item open transfer post-test; PPT significantly higher transfer, marginally higher retention

constructs.label: cybersickness & physical discomfort
constructs.treatment: not directly measured; novelty effect (HMD/controller unfamiliarity) raised as an unmeasured candidate confound

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: not operationalized as a variable; content/script/graphics held constant across media as an imperfect control, per Clark & Feldon (2014) media-comparison critique

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.design: HTC Vive running The Body VR: Journey into a Cell; ~12-min narrated interactive tour with limited object interaction; continuous (IVRn) or 6-segment oral-practice-question (IVRp) delivery
conditions.instruments: Witmer & Singer presence scale (adapted); Russell core-affect grid; CTML extraneous/essential/generative load scales; B-Alert X10 EEG (workload, engagement/distraction/sleep-onset states); EDA (SCL, SCR/sec, PTP); ECG (HR, HRV); 16-item retention + 4-item transfer post-test
conditions.effectDirection: IVR > PPT on presence, enjoyment, positive/high-arousal emotion, self-reported extraneous load, EEG-classified boredom proportion; IVR < PPT on transfer (sig.), retention (marginal), EEG high-engagement probability, ideal-workload proportion; no significant IVR/PPT difference on EDA, HR, HRV, essential/generative load, or difficulty/understanding/effort/interest/motivation

conditions.label: 2D video / slideshow / text (desktop PowerPoint)
conditions.design: 24-slide self-paced PowerPoint built from IVR screenshots plus printed transcription of the IVR narration; no return-to-previous-slide; continuous (PPTn) or 6-segment oral-practice-question (PPTp) delivery
conditions.instruments: same instrument battery as the IVR condition (within-study comparator)
conditions.effectDirection: see IVR row — PPT is the comparator pole on every listed contrast

conditions.label: SEM / process model (no media contrast)
conditions.design: not used in this study; mediation instead run as parallel mediation (Hayes PROCESS macro, 5,000 bootstrap samples) on discrete self-report/biometric variables rather than a latent-variable SEM
conditions.instruments: self-reported extraneous load, self-reported positive/high-arousal emotion, EEG high-engagement probability, HRV as candidate mediators of media→retention/transfer
conditions.effectDirection: extraneous load and positive/high-arousal emotion significantly mediate media→retention (both indirect paths sig.); no mediator reaches significance for media→transfer

readings.claim: IVR causes learners to use limited cognitive resources on extraneous cognitive/affective processing that does not support deep learning, as compared to more conventional media (the 'distraction hypothesis').
Self-reported extraneous cognitive load significantly mediates the relationship between instructional medium and retention scores, in the direction IVR → higher load → lower retention.

Self-reported positive/high-arousal emotion also significantly mediates the medium→retention relationship in the same direction, i.e., functions as a distractor rather than facilitator despite being a positive emotional state.
None of the candidate cognitive or affective mediators significantly explain the medium→transfer relationship; the direct effect of medium on transfer remains significant after including mediators.
Adding oral practice-testing questions during the lesson does not significantly improve retention or transfer in either medium, contrary to generative-learning-theory predictions.
IVR's perceptual richness and induced emotional arousal function as 'seductive details' under CTML's coherence principle, consuming cognitive capacity even as they elevate presence and enjoyment.
Replacing conventional declarative-knowledge instruction with IVR of this type is not yet warranted; IVR may better suit spatial/3D-transformation content or pre-training use.
Media-comparison designs like this one confound instructional medium with instructional method (e.g., continuous animation/narration vs. static text), limiting causal attribution to 'medium' per se.

tensions.axis: positive/high-arousal affect as facilitative (proponent view, e.g. Bailenson, Kozhevnikov) vs. positive/high-arousal affect as a significant negative mediator of retention (this study's own finding)
tensions.note: The study's own mediation result complicates a simple 'positive emotion helps learning' story: the same self-reported positive/high-arousal state that IVR reliably elevates is shown to significantly mediate IVR's lower retention scores, i.e., functions as a distractor despite its positive valence.

tensions.axis: retention mediated by cognitive/affective distraction vs. transfer not significantly mediated by any measured process
tensions.note: The distraction-hypothesis mediators work for retention but not transfer, even though the total effect of medium on transfer is larger and more robust than on retention — an unresolved asymmetry the authors do not fully explain.

tensions.axis: media-comparison research as informative about 'medium' vs. media-comparison research as confounding medium with instructional method
tensions.note: The authors' own limitations section concedes the study cannot cleanly separate IVR's continuous-animation/narration format from the IVR label itself, a live methodological debate in this cluster (cf. Mayer et al. 2022 / ped-sec-07's methods-not-media position).
